title: Abrupt light transitions in illuminance and correlated colour temperature result in different temporal dynamics and interindividual variability for sensation, comfort and alertness
research_question: To what extent an abrupt transition from dim to bright light, or from warm to cool light, influences subjective evaluations of comfort and mood as well as subjective and objective measures of alertness, arousal and thermoregulation over time, and to what extent systematic inter-individual variability occurs in these light-induced effects and interactions between illuminance and correlated colour temperature (CCT).

participants.description: 23 healthy participants (13 female; Mage = 23, SDage = 2.0; range = 18–26 years old). None reported visual/auditory deficits or were extreme chronotypes. None used medication other than contraceptive pill or suffered from hypertension/cardiovascular disease. None travelled intercontinentally in the past three months.
participants.recruitment: Recruited via the J.F. Schouten School for User-System Interaction Research database from the Eindhoven University of Technology.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: An office setting with two separate desks in a climate chamber (18.0m² floor area, 2.7m ceiling height, 17.0°C intended air temperature, 18.0°C operative air temperature). mechanisms: Direct visual perception of light properties (brightness, color temperature).
Adaptation of the visual system to new light conditions over time.
Melanopic activation by light influencing alertness and vitality.
Compensatory effort on tasks masking potential performance effects of light.
moderators: Individual differences (for visual comfort in response to illuminance)
implementation_implications: Dynamic light scenarios aimed at enhancing human alertness and vitality require tailoring to the individual to create visually comfortable environments.
Subjective responses to abrupt light transitions emerge immediately and are transient, emphasizing the need for repeated measurements in study protocols.

Objective measures of vigilance, arousal, and thermoregulation may not respond within 45 minutes of an abrupt light transition, suggesting longer exposure durations or different task designs might be needed to observe effects.

limitations: Study conducted in a relatively controlled environment, with two participants simultaneously, potentially impacting concentration on tasks.
Homogeneous sample (predominantly young and healthy) limits generalizability and may have prevented identification of interindividual variability for some outcomes.
Time-of-day effects were controlled within participants but not between, limiting analysis of interaction effects due to power considerations.
Exposure duration of 45 minutes may be too short to observe effects on performance tasks, physiological arousal, and thermal experience.
PVT version employed might not have sufficient variation in parameters (lapses, standard deviation, variability of RT) to yield more insight.

paper_metadata.title: Abrupt light transitions in illuminance and correlated colour temperature result in different temporal dynamics and interindividual variability for sensation, comfort and alertness
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Abrupt light transitions in illuminance and correlated colour temperature result in different temporal dynamics and interindividual variability for sensation, comfort and alertness
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Detailed insights in both visual effects of light and effects beyond vision due to manipulations in illuminance and correlated color temperature (CCT) are needed to optimize study protocols as well as to design light scenarios for practical applications. This study investigated temporal dynamics and interindividual variability in subjective evaluations of sensation, comfort and mood as well as subjective and objective measures of alertness, arousal and thermoregulation following abrupt transitions in illuminance and CCT in a mild cold environment. The results revealed that effects could be uniquely attributed to changes in illuminance or CCT. No interaction effects of illuminance and CCT were found for any of these markers. Responses to the abrupt transitions in illuminance and CCT always occurred immediately and exclusively amongst the subjective measures. Most of these responses diminished over time within the 45-minute light manipulation. In this period, no responses were found for objective measures of vigilance, arousal or thermoregulation. Significant interindividual variability occurred only in the visual comfort evaluation in response to changes in the intensity of the light. The results indicate that the design of dynamic light scenarios aimed to enhance human alertness and vitality requires tailoring to the individual to create visually comfortable environments.
